Apple___Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Leaves may twist, turn yellow, and drop prematurely.
Apple___Apple_scab.causes: Fungus Venturia inaequalis. Thrives in cool, wet spring weather and overwinters in dead fallen leaves.
precautions: Apply fungicide before major rain events during leaf emergence
Avoid spraying in direct sunlight to avoid leaf scorching
Rotate fungicide classes to prevent resistance
preventionTips: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Prune tree canopy to maximize air circulation and sunlight
Plant resistant cultivars such as Liberty, Freedom, or Enterprise

Apple___Black_rot.symptoms: Small purple flecks on leaves expanding into circular spots with brown centers ('frogeye' spots). Fruit develops firm, concentric brown rings rotting entirely black.
Apple___Black_rot.causes: Fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. Enters through bark wounds, mummified fruits, and dead wood.
precautions: Remove dead wood only during dry winter dormancy
Clean pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol between cuts
preventionTips: Prune out dead or fire-blighted twigs
Remove and bury all mummified apples remaining on the tree or ground
Protect trees from mechanical injuries and insect bores

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surfaces that enlarge and develop tiny black specks. Tube-like fungal projections form on the leaf undersides.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.causes: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae fungus. Requires both apple/crabapple and Eastern red cedar (Juniperus) to complete its lifecycle.
organicRemedies: Sulfur sprays applied from tight cluster through petal fall
Copper fungicides applied at pink bud stage
precautions: Timing is critical: sprays must be applied between bud break and 2 weeks post-bloom
Wear respirator and protective goggles when spraying
preventionTips: Remove nearby Eastern red cedar or juniper trees within a 1-mile radius if possible
Select rust-immune apple varieties like Freedom, Liberty, or William's Pride
Inspect nearby junipers and prune out reddish-brown galls before spring rains

Apple___healthy.symptoms: Vibrant, green foliage with smooth leaf margins and no fungal spots, lesions, or curling.
Apple___healthy.causes: None. The plant is currently healthy and thriving.
pesticides: None needed. Do not apply synthetic fungicides to healthy trees.
organicRemedies: Compost tea soil drench for maintaining beneficial leaf microbiome
Fish amino acid or seaweed extract foliar tonic
precautions: Monitor weekly during spring flush for aphid or caterpillar infestation
Ensure balanced soil nitrogen to prevent succulent susceptible growth
preventionTips: Maintain drip irrigation near drip line, avoiding wetting foliage
Apply 3 inches of organic mulch around root zone
Practice seasonal pruning to maintain open canopy structure

Blueberry___healthy.symptoms: Deep green, glossy foliage with vigorous shoot growth and no wilting or spotting.
organicRemedies: Soil application of acidic pine needle mulch or pine bark
Foliar kelp extract to support natural plant immunity
precautions: Maintain strict soil pH between 4.5 and 5.2
Avoid chlorinated city water if pH is alkaline
preventionTips: Apply elemental sulfur periodically to regulate soil acidity
Maintain consistent soil moisture with pine bark mulch
Prune older canes older than 6 years to stimulate productive shoots

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White to light grayish talcum-like powdery patches on leaves, young twigs, and fruit. Leaves may cup, curl, or stunt.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.causes: Podosphaera clandestina fungus. Favored by warm temperatures with high relative humidity and shaded canopies.
organicRemedies: Neem oil / horticultural mineral oil at 1-2% dilution
Dilute milk spray (40% milk, 60% water) in sunlight
precautions: Do not apply sulfur when temperatures exceed 30°C (85°F) to avoid phytotoxicity
Avoid combining oils with sulfur within 14 days
preventionTips: Prune tree center to allow ample air flow and sunlight penetration
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation
Inspect young water sprouts and prune susceptible shoots

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.symptoms: Lush green leaves, clean bark, no fungal mildew, oozing gummosis, or shot-hole lesions.
organicRemedies: Bio-stimulant seaweed spray to promote cell wall thickness
precautions: Avoid damaging bark during weeding or mechanical trimming
preventionTips: Paint base of trunk with white diluted latex to prevent winter sunscald
Apply dormant copper spray in late autumn after leaf drop to protect bud scars

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.symptoms: Tan or gray rectangular leaf lesions strictly bounded by leaf veins, creating a blocky striped appearance.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.causes: Cercospora zeae-maydis fungus. Overwinters on corn residue; favored by prolonged warm, overcast, and humid conditions.
organicRemedies: Copper sulfate spray during early vegetative stage
precautions: Fungicide application is most economical between VT (tasseling) and R2 (blister stage) when conditions favor disease
preventionTips: Rotate crops with non-host species (Soybean, Alfalfa, or Wheat) for at least 1-2 years
Shred and bury crop residue deep in soil post-harvest
Plant certified hybrids with high Gray Leaf Spot resistance rating

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.symptoms: Cinnamon-brown to reddish, powdery, oval to elongate pustules scattered on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.causes: Puccinia sorghi fungus. Spores are blown northward by wind currents from subtropical regions.
organicRemedies: Sulfur dust or wettable sulfur applied early morning
Compost extract containing antagonistic Pseudomonas species
precautions: Scout fields when 6 or more pustules appear per leaf prior to tasseling
Follow proper PPE when spraying tall corn stands
preventionTips: Plant resistant corn hybrids
Early planting to allow plants to mature before rust spores arrive on seasonal winds
Balanced nitrogen and potassium nutrition

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Long, elliptical grayish-green or cigar-shaped lesions (1 to 6 inches long) that become tan and dry. In damp conditions, dark olivaceous spores form inside lesions.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.causes: Exserohilum turcicum fungus. Overwinters in corn residue, favored by moderate temperatures (18-27°C) and heavy dew.
precautions: Target spray application at the tassel emergence stage if lesions are present on lower third of plant
preventionTips: Plant tolerant or resistant hybrid seed
Practice conservation tillage that buries corn debris or 2-year crop rotation
Maintain optimal plant spacing to avoid prolonged canopy wetness

Corn_(maize)___healthy.symptoms: Broad, deep green leaves with strong stalk development, clear silks, and no necrotic lesions or rust pustules.
precautions: Monitor nitrogen levels to avoid yellowing of lower leaf midribs
Ensure proper drainage during heavy monsoon showers
preventionTips: Soil testing before planting to optimize N-P-K and zinc ratios
Regular field scouting during vegetative growth (V4 to V12 stages)

Grape___Black_rot.symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with tiny black pycnidia specks arranged in rings. Berries turn purplish-brown, shrivel, and dry into hard black mummies.
Grape___Black_rot.causes: Guignardia bidwellii fungus. Overwinters in mummified berries and cane lesions.
organicRemedies: Pure Neem oil spray during bud swell
precautions: Critical protection period is from early bloom through 4-5 weeks post-bloom
Do not apply copper under cool, slow-drying conditions to avoid fruit russeting
preventionTips: Prune out and destroy all mummified grape clusters and infected canes
Trellis and canopy management to promote rapid air drying of leaves
Weed management under the vine trellis

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between veins on older leaves. Berries develop small, dark-brown to purple spots ('measles') and may crack.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).causes: Complex of wood-rotting fungal pathogens (Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Fomitiporia mediterranea) entering pruning wounds.
pesticides: Wound sealants containing benomyl or pyraclostrobin applied immediately to large cuts.
organicRemedies: Sodium silicate foliar applications to strengthen cell walls
precautions: Avoid pruning during wet or rainy weather when spores are actively dispersed
Disinfect pruning tools with bleach or alcohol between vines
preventionTips: Double-pruning practice: rough prune early, final prune late in dormant season
Protect all pruning cuts greater than 2cm with pruning paste or paint
Replace severely infected dying vines with certified clean nursery stock

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.symptoms: Irregular, angular, dark brown to black spots on leaves often bordered by veins. Severe infections cause premature defoliation in late summer.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.causes: Pseudocercospora cladosporioides (Isariopsis clavispora) fungus. Thrives in warm, humid weather.
organicRemedies: Foliar application of bio-fungicide Bacillus subtilis
precautions: Ensure thorough coverage of both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Observe 14-day pre-harvest interval for copper sprays
preventionTips: Promptly remove and compost or burn fallen infected leaves
Open up the grapevine canopy by shoot thinning and lateral leaf removal around fruiting zone
Maintain balanced vine vigor

Grape___healthy.symptoms: Uniform emerald-green palmate leaves, vigorous vine tendrils, and clean developing clusters.
organicRemedies: Compost mulch along the vineyard rows
precautions: Avoid excessive synthetic nitrogen fertilizers that cause dense, disease-prone shading
preventionTips: Establish good trellis architecture (e.g., Vertical Shoot Positioning)
Manage cover crops between rows to encourage beneficial predator insects

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy yellow mottling across leaf veins (unlike symmetrical nutrient deficiencies). Yellow shoots, small lopsided bitter fruit that remains green at base.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, transmitted by the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri) vector.
organicRemedies: Kaolin clay (Surround WP) foliar barrier against psyllids
Horticultural mineral oil (1-2%) to deter egg-laying psyllids
precautions: No curative cure exists for infected trees; management focuses on insect vector suppression and tree removal
Check quarantine rules before moving citrus plants
preventionTips: Plant only certified disease-free citrus trees from state-registered nurseries
Aggressively scout and spray psyllid populations during young flush growth
Immediately remove and destroy confirmed infected trees to protect surrounding orchards

Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked, angular, dark brown spots on leaves that fall out, giving a 'shot-hole' appearance. Fruit develops pitted dark sunken craters.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Spread by wind-driven rain and dew.
organicRemedies: Low-rate fixed copper sprays during dormant season and early petal fall
precautions: Excessive copper on peach foliage can cause severe leaf burning; strictly monitor chemical dosage and stage
Avoid spraying in humid overcast conditions that delay drying
preventionTips: Plant resistant peach cultivars (e.g., Clayton, Biscoe, Harrow Beauty)
Avoid planting in light sandy soils prone to wind erosion which damages leaves
Prune to open center architecture for fast drying

Peach___healthy.symptoms: Lanceolate, glossy dark green foliage with smooth margins and no gumming, curl, or shot holes.
organicRemedies: Seaweed extract and micronutrient foliar spray (zinc and boron)
precautions: Protect fruit from bird and insect punctures during ripening
preventionTips: Apply dormant copper spray in late autumn to prevent peach leaf curl in spring
Thin fruit to 6 inches apart to maximize fruit size and tree vitality

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots that turn brownish-black with a yellowish halo. Leaves turn yellow and drop. Fruit displays raised, warty, scab-like spots.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas euvesicatoria. Spreads rapidly in warm, rainy weather via water droplets and handling.
precautions: Never enter or harvest pepper fields when plants are wet with dew or rain
Disinfect stakes, trays, and tools with 10% sodium hypochlorite
preventionTips: Use only certified pathogen-free, hot-water treated seeds
Rotate fields out of solanaceous crops (peppers, tomatoes, eggplants) for at least 3 years
Utilize drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers to keep foliage dry

Pepper,_bell___healthy.symptoms: Smooth, rich green leaves, sturdy stems with erect habit, and glossy firm bell pepper fruit.
organicRemedies: Compost tea and vermicompost soil dressing
Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate) foliar mist to support chlorophyll
precautions: Maintain regular watering to avoid calcium deficiency blossom end rot
preventionTips: Mulch with straw or black plastic to regulate soil temperature and conserve moisture
Install sturdy stakes or cages to support heavy fruit load

Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown to black circular lesions displaying distinctive concentric rings ('target-board' or 'bullseye' pattern) on older lower leaves. Surrounding tissue turns yellow.
Potato___Early_blight.causes: Fungus Alternaria solani. Favored by alternating periods of heavy dew/rain and warm dry sunny days.
organicRemedies: Neem oil spray (0.5% concentration) applied every 7-10 days
precautions: Alternate fungicide chemical modes of action (FRAC codes) to prevent fungicide resistance
Avoid applying under high noon heat to prevent foliar phytotoxicity
preventionTips: Rotate potatoes with non-solanaceous crops such as corn, pulses, or cereals for 3 years
Ensure balanced potassium and nitrogen fertility to maintain plant vigor
Use certified disease-free seed tubers

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked dark brown to purplish-black lesions that spread quickly. In humid mornings, a white cottony fungal mold appears on leaf undersides. Stem lesions blacken and tubers rot.
Potato___Late_blight.causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans (the pathogen of the Irish Potato Famine). Explodes under cool (15-20°C), wet, foggy weather.
precautions: Late blight moves aggressively: initiate preventive sprays immediately when weather forecast indicates continuous dampness
Destroy infected haulms before harvest to prevent tuber contamination
preventionTips: Plant certified blight-resistant potato cultivars
Eliminate all potato cull piles and volunteer potato sprouts in spring
Hill soil properly around potato stems to create a physical barrier preventing spores from washing into tubers

Potato___healthy.symptoms: Uniform deep green foliage, robust compound leaves with no target spots, water-soaking, or leaf curl.
organicRemedies: Humic acid and organic seaweed soil conditioner
precautions: Avoid waterlogging in heavy soils which induces root asphyxiation
preventionTips: Maintain 1.5 inches of water per week through tuber bulking
Hill up soil around plants twice during the vegetative cycle

Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Vibrant serrated leaves, upright canes, vigorous floricane and primocane growth without spur blight or rust.
organicRemedies: Wood chip mulch to protect shallow feeder roots
Organic fish emulsion foliar feed in early spring
precautions: Do not plant raspberries near wild brambles or solanaceous vegetables
preventionTips: Prune spent floricanes down to the ground immediately after summer harvest
Trellis canes to keep foliage and berries well elevated above damp soil

Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Clean trifoliate green leaves, sturdy branching, healthy pink-interior nitrogen-fixing root nodules, no rust or mosaic.
precautions: Scout weekly during flowering (R1-R3) for defoliating caterpillars and stink bugs
preventionTips: Incorporate balanced crop rotation with corn or wheat
Plant at recommended row spacing to ensure early canopy closure which shades out competitive weeds

Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery talcum-powder spots on upper and lower surfaces of leaves and stems. Affected leaves turn yellow, brown, and brittle, exposing fruit to sunscald.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.causes: Podosphaera xanthii fungus. Spreads rapidly in dense foliage in dry weather with high humidity.
organicRemedies: Diluted baking soda spray (1 tbsp baking soda + 1 tsp horticultural soap in 1 gallon water)
precautions: Ensure complete coverage of leaf undersides where mildew colonies initiate
Apply sprays early in the morning before strong direct sunlight
preventionTips: Choose powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties (PMR)
Provide generous spacing between plants (3-4 feet) for ample airflow
Use drip irrigation to keep cucurbit leaves completely dry

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Irregular purplish to dark brown blotches on upper leaf surfaces. As spots coalesce, whole leaves turn purplish, brown, and curl upwards, appearing burned or scorched.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.causes: Diplocarpon earlianum fungus. Spores splash onto foliage from infected overwintering crowns.
organicRemedies: Copper hydroxide fungicide applied after harvest renovation
Garlic extract spray as an organic antifungal preventative
precautions: Renovate strawberry beds promptly after harvest to remove scorched foliage
Do not apply certain fungicides during peak bee pollination
preventionTips: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runners
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; switch to drip tape under straw mulch
Mow, rake, and burn old leaves after the final harvest of June-bearing varieties

Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Bright emerald green trifoliate leaves, robust crowns, clean white flowers, and symmetrical plump red berries.
organicRemedies: Clean pine straw mulch underneath crowns
Foliar calcium and boron spray to improve fruit firmness and cell wall strength
precautions: Keep berries elevated off direct wet soil with clean straw bedding
preventionTips: Plant on raised beds to ensure rapid water drainage
Remove runner plants to focus mother plant energy into crown development

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked, dark brown circular to angular spots with greasy appearance on leaves. Leaf tissue between spots may turn yellow and drop. Fruits develop small raised black scabs.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas perforans / Xanthomonas vesicatoria. Spreads via splashing rain, overhead irrigation, and contaminated tools.
pesticides: Copper hydroxide combined with Mancozeb (increases bioavailable copper ions)
organicRemedies: Hydrogen peroxide + peracetic acid foliage spray (OxiDate)
precautions: Do not work in tomato rows when leaves are wet with morning dew or rain
Sanitize all pruning scissors and trellising stakes
preventionTips: Use certified disease-free seeds or perform hot-water seed treatment (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding peppers and potatoes
Switch to drip irrigation and mulch beds with wheat straw or black plastic

Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown circular spots with concentric target-like rings on older lower leaves. Leaves turn yellow around spots and drop. Stem lesions are dark and elongated.
Tomato___Early_blight.causes: Fungus Alternaria solani. Overwinters on infected plant debris and soil.
organicRemedies: Neem oil spray (0.5% concentration every 7 days)
precautions: Prune lower leaves that touch the ground to stop soil-splashed spores
Spray early in the morning so leaves dry quickly in the sun
Rotate fungicide chemical groups to prevent resistance
preventionTips: Remove infected leaves immediately and dispose of outside the garden
Avoid excess watering and overhead sprinkling
Maintain proper plant spacing (45-60 cm) for air circulation
Mulch base of tomato plants to prevent soil splash

Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large, dark water-soaked greasy gray-green lesions on leaves and stems. White fluffy mold develops on leaf undersides in humid mornings. Fruit turns brown with firm greasy rot.
Tomato___Late_blight.causes: Oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Spreads rapidly in cool (15-22°C), humid, and rainy weather.
precautions: Act immediately: late blight can destroy an entire tomato field within 72 hours of outbreak
Destroy heavily blighted plants completely; do not compost them
preventionTips: Plant blight-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant, Legend)
Ensure wide spacing and high staking for good ventilation
Never plant tomatoes adjacent to potato patches

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale greenish-yellow chlorotic spots with indefinite margins on upper leaf surfaces. Dense olive-green to velvety brown mold layers appear on the corresponding undersides.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.causes: Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum) fungus. Prevalent in greenhouses and high tunnels with relative humidity above 85%.
precautions: Maximize ventilation in polyhouses and polytunnels to lower relative humidity below 80%
Prune bottom suckers and lower foliage to promote airflow
preventionTips: Install circulating exhaust fans in greenhouse structures
Water strictly via drip lines at ground level
Grow resistant tomato hybrids containing Cf resistance genes

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Numerous small circular spots (1-3 mm) with dark brown borders and lighter gray or tan centers containing tiny black specks (pycnidia). Progresses from bottom leaves upwards.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici. Spores survive in solanaceous weed debris and splash onto leaves.
organicRemedies: Neem oil 1% emulsified with mild soap
precautions: Avoid working in the field when plants are wet
Thoroughly sterilize plant stakes and cages at end of season
preventionTips: Apply 3-4 inches of straw mulch immediately after transplanting
Prune lower 12 inches of foliage as plants grow
Eradicate horsenettle and nightshade weeds near tomato beds

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Yellow or white stippling (tiny speckled dots) on upper leaf surfaces. Fine silken webbing on leaf undersides and stems. Severe infestation leads to bronze, dry, paper-like leaves.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.causes: Tetranychus urticae (Two-spotted spider mite). Populations explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions (temperatures > 30°C).
organicRemedies: Insecticidal soap spray targeting leaf undersides
Neem oil (1-2%) or pure Karanja oil spray
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus)
precautions: Avoid broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids which kill beneficial predatory insects and cause mite population resurgence
Direct spray nozzles upwards to hit leaf undersides
preventionTips: Keep farm pathways damp to suppress road dust
Hose down foliage periodically with a strong stream of water to dislodge mites
Maintain adequate crop hydration to reduce plant stress

Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small brown water-soaked spots with dark margins and concentric rings that can crack open. Lesions also attack stems, pedicels, and fruit.
Tomato___Target_Spot.causes: Corynespora cassiicola fungus. Thrives in warm, humid tropical and subtropical climates.
precautions: Do not crowd plants; adequate spacing is essential
Rotate fungicide classes to prevent fungal resistance
preventionTips: Destroy all crop debris immediately after harvest
Prune lower tomato suckers to improve aeration
Maintain 3-year field rotation

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Severe upward cupping and curling of leaf margins, reduced leaf size, chlorosis (yellowing) between veins, stunted bushy plant growth, and massive flower drop.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.causes: Begomovirus transmitted exclusively by the Silverleaf Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). Not seed-transmitted.
organicRemedies: Yellow sticky insect traps placed at canopy height
Neem oil spray (1.5%) combined with insecticidal soap against whitefly nymphs
precautions: There is no chemical cure once a plant is infected with the virus; all treatments focus on whitefly control
Remove and bag virus-infected plants immediately to stop vector feeding
preventionTips: Plant certified TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tycoon, Securitas, SV0224TM)
Cover seedlings with insect-proof floating row covers during first 30 days
Eradicate alternate weed hosts (nightshades, mallows, datura) near tomato fields

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, distortion ('fern-leaf' or strap-like leaves), leaf wrinkling, and stunted growth. Fruit shows internal brown browning.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.causes: Tobamovirus. Extremely stable virus transmitted mechanically via hands, tools, grafting, and tobacco products. Survives in seed coats and soil.
pesticides: No antiviral pesticides exist. Focus on strict sanitation and viral vector hygiene.
organicRemedies: Wash hands with 20% non-fat dry milk solution before handling plants to neutralize virus particles
Bio-stimulant chitosan spray to induce systemic acquired resistance (SAR)
precautions: Workers who smoke or handle tobacco must wash hands with soap and water before touching tomato plants
Disinfect tools with trisodium phosphate (TSP) or 20% skimmed milk
preventionTips: Plant certified virus-resistant cultivars (look for 'ToMV' or 'TMV' on seed packets)
Use certified hot-water or TSP-treated seeds
Carefully rogue out and incinerate infected plants upon initial symptom detection

Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Deep emerald-green compound leaves, robust hairy stems, bright yellow flowers, and firm, smooth unblemished tomatoes.
Tomato___healthy.causes: None. Plant is healthy and vigorous.
pesticides: None needed. Do not apply chemical fungicides.
organicRemedies: Compost tea soil drench every 14 days
Foliar spray of diluted seaweed liquid for micronutrient vitality
precautions: Avoid touching plants when foliage is wet from morning dew
preventionTips: Stake or trellis vines to keep fruit and leaves elevated above soil
Maintain consistent soil moisture with drip irrigation to avoid blossom end rot
Mulch around base with 2 inches of organic straw or woodchips
